# Turn Voice Memos into Clear Notes with Apple Intelligence

**By the end of this guide, you'll be able to record a thought on your iPhone, get a written transcript of it, and have Apple Intelligence turn that transcript into a clean, short summary — perfect for saving, sharing, or finding later.**

## Before you start
- An **iPhone 15 Pro, 15 Pro Max, 16, 16 Pro or newer** (or an iPad/Mac with an M1 chip or later). Apple Intelligence only runs on these devices.
- **iOS 18.1, iPadOS 18.1 or macOS Sequoia 15.1** (or newer). Update in **Settings > General > Software Update** if needed.
- **Apple Intelligence turned on** — go to **Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri** and follow the prompts. The first-time setup can take a few minutes.
- The **Voice Memos** app (pre-installed) and the **Notes** app (also pre-installed).
- Around **5 to 10 minutes** in total. The feature is free — no paid plan needed.

## Step 1 — Open Voice Memos and start recording
Tap the **Voice Memos** icon on your Home Screen. The app opens to your list of past recordings (or a clean screen if it's your first time). Look at the bottom-centre of the screen and tap the large **red round button with a red dot** inside it. Recording begins right away — a wavy line appears on screen and a small timer starts counting up in the top corner. If the layout looks different on your device, look for a button labelled **"Record"** or an icon shaped like a microphone.
💬 Example: you might say out loud, "Just a quick note about the school fundraiser — follow up with the venue on Monday, and confirm the caterer by Wednesday."
You'll know it worked when the timer is counting and the red waveform is moving on the screen.

## Step 2 — Speak clearly at a natural pace
Hold the phone about **15 to 20 cm from your mouth** (roughly a hand's length) and talk as if you were explaining your idea to a friend. The waveform will jump higher when you speak and flatten during pauses, so you can see it's picking you up. Try to avoid rustling paper or tapping the phone while you talk, because that adds noise. If your recording is meant for someone else, imagine they're listening — short, complete sentences are easier to transcribe than one long run-on thought.
💬 Example: "Pick up dry cleaning, email the vet about the dog's vaccination, and start drafting the new brochure tonight."
You'll know it worked when the recording continues without dropping out and the waveform reacts to every sentence you say.

## Step 3 — Stop the recording and give it a useful name
Tap the **red square stop button** (it replaces the record button while you're recording). The app saves your memo straight away and shows a label called **"New Recording"** at the top. Tap that label and type in a real name so you can find it later. Renaming only takes a second and saves you a lot of scrolling when you have dozens of memos. If your version doesn't show a name field at the top, look for a small **"⋯" menu** inside the recording and choose **"Edit Recording"** or **"Rename"**.
💬 Example: name it "School fundraiser tasks" or "Ideas for Sunday lunch".
You'll know it worked when you see your recording in the list with the new name sitting above the date and length.

## Step 4 — Open the written transcript
Tap on your saved recording to open it. You'll see the play button and a waveform at the top of the screen. Now look just below that for a **small transcript button** — it often looks like a little speech bubble, an "Aa" icon, or three short lines of text. Tap it, and after a moment a written version of what you said appears, with each word synced to the audio. You can tap any word in the text to jump the playback straight to that point. If you don't see a transcript button on first try, scroll down the page — on some iOS versions it sits further down, or it may be hidden behind a **"⋯" menu** labelled **"Show Transcript"**.
💬 Example: tapping the transcript button on your "School fundraiser tasks" memo reveals a written version of every task you just said out loud.
You'll know it worked when you can read your spoken words as text on the screen and play the audio while following along.

## Step 5 — Copy the transcript and ask Apple Intelligence to summarise
**Long-press** on any word in the transcript, then choose **"Select All"** followed by **"Copy"** from the pop-up menu. Open the **Notes** app, start a **new note**, and **paste** the text in. Tap inside the text so the keyboard appears, and you'll see a small toolbar above the keyboard with Apple Intelligence tools. Look for a button labelled **"Summarise"** (or a sparkle ✨ icon labelled **"Writing Tools"**). Tap it and choose **"Summarise"**. Apple Intelligence will read your transcript and replace the long version with a short summary — usually two to four bullet points or a short paragraph. If the summary isn't quite right, you can try again, or pick a different style like **"Key Points"** or **"Make Shorter"**.
💬 Example: after pasting a 200-word rambling about your fundraiser, you tap Summarise and get: "Three actions: call the venue Monday, confirm the caterer Wednesday, start the brochure tonight."
You'll know it worked when a shorter, organised version of your transcript appears in the note, ready to read, search, or share.

## Step 6 — Review, tidy up, and save
Read the summary once from top to bottom. Apple Intelligence usually captures the gist, but it can miss a small detail or phrase something awkwardly — quick edits now will save confusion later. Add or remove anything important, then **tap "Done"** in the top-right corner (or just close the note — Notes auto-saves). Your summary now lives in Notes, where you can search it, share it with a tap, or set a reminder against it. If you also want the original transcript kept, leave it in the same note below the summary, separated by a heading.
💬 Example: add the missing line "Plus remind Tom to bring chairs" right under the three bullet points before tapping Done.
You'll know it worked when you can find your summary again by searching Notes, and when reading it takes only a few seconds instead of listening to the full memo.

## Common mistakes
- **Recording in a noisy room.** Loud music, traffic, or other voices make transcripts messy. Move somewhere quieter, or hold the mic closer to your mouth.
- **Forgetting to turn on Apple Intelligence.** If the Summarise button never appears, go to **Settings > Apple Intelligence & Siri** and make sure it's actually switched on. The very first setup can take several minutes in the background.
- **Trusting the summary blindly.** Apple Intelligence is good at shortening, but it can drop a small but important detail. Always read the summary once and add anything that's missing before you share it.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Capture sudden ideas, shopping lists, or reminders while you're walking, cooking, or in the car — then have them waiting as tidy, searchable notes by the time you sit down.
- **For your business or work:** Record a quick meeting or brainstorm on your phone, and within a couple of minutes have a clean written summary to send to your team or drop into a project doc.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick the next idea that pops into your head, record a 30-second voice memo about it, and run it through Step 5. After one try, the habit tends to stick on its own.

## Try it now
Record a 30-second voice memo right now about anything on your mind — what you did today, a thought about a project, or a reminder for tomorrow. Then follow Step 5 and watch Apple Intelligence summarise it in a few seconds.
